title: The great Buddha of Nara
hookLine: an emperor asks everyone, down to a handful of earth, to help cast a giant bronze Buddha

lines: A KNEE HIGHER THAN YOUR HEAD.
cards: The doors of the hall swing open, and at first the eyes don't know what they're looking at. A bronze knee, higher than your head. A hand raised, palm out, bigger than a person.
Far above, in the dim light, a calm face looks down over everyone who walks in. Schoolchildren crane their necks. Deer wander outside the gate.
This is Todaiji, in Nara, and the seated figure inside is the great Buddha.

teach.b: Japan's official chronicle, the Shoku Nihongi, preserves Emperor Shomu's edict calling for the image. He says he has the wealth and the power of the land, and could simply order it made.
But that, he says, would miss the point. So he asks that anyone who wishes to help, even by bringing a single branch of grass or a handful of earth, be allowed to share in the work.
A giant made of countless small offerings.
The great Buddha is Vairocana, called Rushana in Japanese, the Buddha at the center of the Flower Garland Sutra, the same sutra behind the Huayan school Uisang carried home to Korea.
In Japan that school is called Kegon, and Todaiji became its great temple. In the sutra, Vairocana's light reaches into every world. A Buddha that large is trying to show something that large.
When the image was finished, a ceremony was held to open its eyes, with an Indian monk, Bodhisena, holding the brush.
Cords tied to the brush ran out into the crowd, so many hands could hold them and share in the moment.
Fire and war have damaged the image more than once, and the head you see today is a later recasting, not the first one.
Through every repair, the expression stayed the same kind: not triumphant, calm. Vast things can be frightening, the sea at night, the sky over a desert.
Here vastness is shown at peace, a hand raised as if to say, don't be afraid.

how: Todaiji in Nara is still a working temple of the Kegon school, where pilgrims and visitors come to bow before the great Buddha, and monks hold regular services in the hall.

games.why: his edict asks that anyone who wishes, even bringing a branch of grass or a handful of earth, share in the work.

practice: Bring to mind the biggest thing you've ever stood in front of, an ocean, a mountain, a night sky, a canyon, and notice the body's first response, a tightening or a widening.
Then let it be calm, the way the bronze face is calm, and breathe inside that size.

wordCard.voice: Vairocana. The great Buddha of Nara, cast in bronze at Todaiji with the help of anyone who brought a handful of earth, vast and at peace.

carryVoice: Your line: vast and calm. A giant, made of handfuls of earth. See you tomorrow.
